html:
The map's label for foraging peoples of the high, dry and cold parts of the Andes that lay outside the farming states, shown from 1500 BCE to 1715. The label is broad; it mostly marks the southern Andes and the high puna grasslands of what is now northern Chile and Argentina.

People had lived in the high Andes since the end of the Ice Age, using caves and rock shelters at great heights. They hunted vicuña and guanaco, the wild relatives of the llama, along with deer and smaller game, and gathered roots and seeds. Many painted or carved animals and hunting scenes on rock walls.

Further north, in the central Andes, hunters tamed wild camelids into the llama and alpaca, and farmers bred the potato and quinoa. That led to herding villages such as Wankarani and later to states like Tiwanaku and the Inca Empire. Where the land was harsher, hunting and herding stayed the main way of life, and peoples moved between the mountains and the valleys of the Andean states and chiefdoms. In the far south their neighbours included the Mapuche.
